response:
Mixture-of-Experts models route each token to a small subset of specialized expert networks, and the central question here is: when your token distribution has a heavy tail — rare tokens, domain-specific jargon, low-frequency syntactic constructions — do those tokens systematically land on the same few experts, and what happens to those experts and the ones they avoid? The key concepts are the routing function (typically a learned gating network with top-k selection), load balancing losses that penalize expert popularity imbalance, and the distinction between routing collapse (all tokens converge to one or two experts) and the subtler tail-token clustering where only rare tokens collapse while common tokens distribute fine, making standard balance metrics look healthy. A beginner sees load-balancing loss go down and concludes training is stable; an expert checks whether that balance metric is aggregated over a batch dominated by head-distribution tokens, which can mask total starvation of certain experts on tail inputs specifically. The deeper worry is that collapsed routing on tail tokens is self-reinforcing: an expert that rarely receives rare-token gradients stays undertrained on them, which makes the router increasingly prefer other experts for those tokens, which further starves the first expert — a feedback loop invisible in aggregate metrics until you probe per-token-frequency routing distributions separately. This matters operationally because tail tokens are often exactly where you need expert specialization most (technical vocabulary, code edge cases, low-resource language fragments), so collapse there degrades the model precisely where MoE's capacity advantage was supposed to help.

The first diagnostic is a per-expert routing frequency histogram stratified by token frequency bin — concretely, bucket your vocabulary by corpus frequency (e.g., top 1K, 1K–10K, 10K–100K, tail >100K rank), then for each bin compute the empirical routing distribution across experts and measure its entropy. Legitimate specialization produces different low-entropy distributions across bins — rare tokens route to expert 7, common tokens route to expert 3 — whereas collapse produces the same low-entropy distribution: everything, regardless of frequency bin, piles into expert 2. The second diagnostic is expert gradient norm disaggregated by token frequency: in legitimate specialization, expert 7 should show healthy gradient signal specifically from tail tokens; in collapse, tail tokens arrive at an expert that's already saturated with head-token gradients, and the tail-specific gradient contribution is negligible — you can measure this by masking the loss to only tail tokens and logging per-expert gradient norms. The data slice you want is a held-out tail-heavy evaluation set — Gopher's work on dataset mixture and Switch Transformer's auxiliary loss ablations both illustrate how aggregate metrics hide this, so you need a slice where >80% of tokens fall below your frequency threshold. Concretely in Switch Transformer (Fedus et al., 2021), the auxiliary load-balancing loss coefficient was tuned against overall token balance, but nothing in that objective explicitly protects tail bins; a routing entropy gap larger than ~1.5 nats between head and tail bins on the same expert set is a reasonable empirical alarm threshold. Finally, compare expert assignment consistency across two passes of the same tail token in dropout-off eval: high variance in routing for identical rare tokens indicates the gating network hasn't converged on a representation for them, which is a collapse precursor distinct from stable specialization.

The contradiction is real and structural: upper layers are where token representations have collapsed low-frequency surface variation into high-level semantic geometry, which is precisely where expert specialization yields the most leverage, but it's also where a 10-step-stale hidden state looks most alien to the current model — so replay-based remediation is maximally corrupted exactly where it's most needed, confirming that replay buffers are probably the wrong tool for upper-layer tail experts specifically. The implication for routing placement is that MoE layers should not be uniformly distributed for tail-heavy distributions — the empirical case for this comes from GLaM (Du et al., 2021) and Mixtral analyses showing that routing decisions in lower-middle layers (roughly 30-60% of depth) tend to be more stable and content-addressable, while upper-layer routing is more context-sensitive and volatile, suggesting a design where tail-sensitive MoE layers are concentrated in the middle of the stack where representations are semantically rich but not yet maximally context-entangled. A concrete architectural proposal following this logic is layer-stratified expert assignment: fix head-token experts in upper layers (where context-sensitivity benefits frequent, syntactically complex tokens most) and fix tail-token experts in middle layers (where semantic content is stable enough for replay and specialization), with upper layers using dense computation or very wide top-k routing for tail tokens rather than sparse dispatch. This connects to findings in probing studies (Tenney et al., 2019 on BERT; analogous results in decoder-only models) showing that lexical and morphological features — the features most diagnostic for rare tokens — peak in middle layers, not upper layers, which suggests middle-layer MoE routing is actually better aligned with what tail tokens need to be routed on. The practical implication is that the standard practice of placing MoE layers at every transformer block (as in Switch Transformer) or at alternating blocks (as in Mixtral) is not principled with respect to tail distributions — a heterogeneous stack with dense upper layers and sparse middle layers would be more robust, at the cost of breaking the clean architectural uniformity that makes current implementations tractable. The deeper theoretical point is that routing placement is currently treated as an engineering convenience rather than a function of what information is available at each layer to make a good routing decision, and for tail tokens specifically, the routing signal degrades monotonically with depth in a way that has not been measured or optimized in any published system.
